findings.title: Game capture observer disables a microphone enabled through the mixer
findings.severity: P1 user-visible audio loss; high confidence, no secret disclosure
findings.confidence: confirmed source and reproduced with external Go overlay / loopback OBS fixture
findings.trigger: The saved legacy deck.json microphone setting is false (the default); the player separately enables microphone_enabled in mixer.json. applyMixer/ensureAudio enable the source in all managed scenes. A game capture observer cycle rebuilds the idle scene or establishes a game target.
findings.impact: sceneVideoWhitelist consults Settings.Microphone instead of the effective mixer preference and removes MicAudio from the keep set. The watcher disables the microphone scene item in IdleScene and GameScene while mixer preferences/source mute can still report microphone enabled/unmuted. Broadcasts, recordings and replay can silently lose microphone audio on game transitions. The reproduction starts with enabled scene items, retains microphone_enabled=true, and observes both scene items disabled.

observed: OBSGod Idle MicAudio scene item disabled by watcher
OBSGod Game MicAudio scene item disabled by watcher

findings.fix_sketch: Resolve effective microphone policy once for a managed video cycle using the same mixer preference source as audio configuration, then preserve its scene membership through idle/game whitelist operations. Keep enable, mute and push-to-talk semantics distinct. Avoid another microphone preference store. Consolidating the effective-policy read is a bounded refactor tied to this defect.
acceptance: Run the actual observer path with legacy microphone=false plus mixer microphone_enabled=true; mic scene items remain connected in game and idle before/after transitions.
Check disabled, explicitly muted and push-to-talk preferences remain muted and never gain an implicit unmute.
Verify game/idle transitions preserve gain, route, source mute and all independent output states; use protocol fixtures during repair and actual audible Deck clip/viewer evidence under #86.

findings.title: Capture observer mutates after its managed collection observation becomes stale
findings.severity: P2 wrong-collection mutation / output scene disruption
findings.confidence: confirmed source and reproduced with external Go overlay / loopback OBS fixture
findings.trigger: After WatchCapture observes the managed profile/collection and active output, delayed game discovery or another process switches OBS to an ordinary collection. No shared control lease or fresh ownership/output observation precedes gameVideoStep.
findings.impact: The observer may issue SetCurrentProgramScene and scene/input mutations against the newly selected collection using its prior snapshot. The loopback reproduction switches collection during discovery and the very next request is SetCurrentProgramScene(OBSGod Idle), with no intervening ownership read. If matching scene names exist, their content or program scene can be changed. This is the same stale-observation boundary that resilience explicitly rechecks; the separate lifetime lease only prevents duplicate watchers.

observed: collection set to Ordinary collection inside discover callback
program scene changed to OBSGod Idle without ownership recheck

findings.fix_sketch: Keep the distinct watcher lifetime lease, but bound delayed discovery and acquire the shared control lease for the mutation phase, then re-observe managed profile/collection and active output immediately before scene/source changes. Explicit operations should win. Preserve a startup readiness handshake so Start waiting for its watcher while holding the control lease cannot deadlock; reuse the resilience observer pattern rather than introducing a new coordination framework.
acceptance: Switch collection/profile or stop output during a blocked discovery callback: no scene/input mutation follows the stale observation.
Hold the shared control lease for an explicit stop/configuration: the watcher yields and later re-observes rather than acting on old state.
Starting output plus attaching the watcher while the initiating command holds its lease remains bounded and does not deadlock.
Retain game-only privacy: no full-display fallback and no automatic output start/restart.

findings.title: Recording lifecycle and runtime reads bypass malformed-output validation
findings.severity: P1 safety invariant / medium-high impact under malformed successful OBS responses
findings.confidence: confirmed source and reproduced with a loopback protocol-only fixture; no real OBS or outputs
findings.trigger: A successful GetRecordStatus response omits or nulls outputActive in RuntimeStatus, the recording start preflight, or a StopRecording preflight/finalization poll. Generated Go bool fields default false.
findings.impact: RuntimeStatus returns recording=false and nil error while recording state is unknown; direct StartRecording can dispatch StartRecord after an unknown preflight. Public API StopRecording can return a supposedly finalized path and nil error while the fixture remains active, because its initial validated APIRecordingStatus does not validate the later lifecycle polls. Managed callers may treat an unknown recording as idle before capture or service configuration. This violates the documented unknown-state and finalized-recording contracts.
findings.fix_sketch: Use one validated recording observation helper for RuntimeStatus and every StartRecording/StopRecording preflight/readback. Require a raw bool outputActive before authorizing or confirming lifecycle actions. Require outputPaused wherever a known paused value is exposed. Keep legacy ACK behavior and safe fixed diagnostics. This is a concrete consolidation of duplicated status decoding rather than a broad framework rewrite.
acceptance: Table-test omitted, null and wrong-type outputActive at each recording lifecycle observation; unknown preflight dispatches no StartRecord or StopRecord.
Malformed finalization polls return an error and no finalized path even after StopRecord ACK; valid delayed shutdown still waits until explicitly inactive.
RuntimeStatus and managed configuration/capture preflights cannot convert unknown recording state into idle authorization.
If outputPaused is exposed as known, omitted/null/wrong-type paused flags remain unknown/error rather than false.
Retain existing stream/record/replay coexistence, partial-media preservation and legacy request-ACK contracts; focused Go protocol/race checks only during repair, final matrix remains #85.

findings.title: SDK response timeouts keep a poisoned public API connection reusable
findings.severity: P2 correctness and interrupted-mutation state safety
findings.confidence: reproduced with a loopback fake OBS and confirmed pinned SDK request-ID FIFO implementation
findings.trigger: An OBS request response arrives after the SDK response timeout but before the longer public operation deadline. Public Connect passes ConnectTimeout into automation.Config.Timeout, which also sets goobs response timeout (defaults3s versus facade15s). The SDK returns an untyped timeout; request projects it to RequestError with Code0; api.run does not invalidate the connection because it only closes context errors.
findings.impact: The first call returns obs_request with no OBS code and Client.Closed remains false despite an interrupted operation. A subsequent mutation is sent on the same connection; the delayed prior response is consumed as its reply and fails the SDK ID check, so the second operation can apply while being reported failed. The connection stays reusable after that error too. SDK ID checking prevents a false successful acknowledgement but does not recover response alignment or establish the unknown mutation outcome.

reproduction.parameters: ConnectTimeout100ms, OperationTimeout1s; fixture applies legacy StartStream then delays its ACK150ms; next legacy StopStream is applied and successfully ACKed. No actual output or OBS process.

findings.fix_sketch: Distinguish SDK transport/response deadline failures from a numeric server request rejection without retaining raw text. Invalidate/close the owned connection on a response timeout or loss of request/response correlation before releasing the public operation lease. Preserve safe timeout/cancellation classification and require reconnect plus observation before retrying. Keep ordinary numeric OBS rejection errors compatible. A small adapter error classification/lifecycle repair suffices; do not replace the transport framework.
acceptance: A delayed-ACK fixture with shorter SDK response budget than public deadline returns a safe timeout/unavailable failure and marks the connection closed.
A subsequent operation on that client is rejected before any new request reaches the fixture; reconnect/observe remains caller-explicit.
A valid numeric OBS rejection preserves obs_request plus its OBS code and need not poison the connection.
Keep caller-deadline cancellation ownership, waiting-cancellation independence, once-only physical close, and no raw endpoint/key/server-message exposure.

findings.title: Unload can exhaust Decky's five-second deadline before cancelling an in-flight Start
findings.trigger: Decky replacement/reload/removal signals a backend with an in-flight Start while dependency.close or microphone talk-cancel is slow. The pinned official loader terminates a still-alive backend after five seconds.
findings.impact: The hook awaits dependency closure and then an eight-second mixer operation before stop() latches cancellation or signals the pending Start. Decky may SIGKILL the Python backend first. Ordinary Go children have no parent-death supervision; the pending action can continue after replacement/removal. The hook's 18/12/12-second waits cannot be relied on under this loader deadline. Hook success also does not drain configuration reader tasks; one can remain pending after unload returns.

reproduction.safety: Fake executable sleeps and writes a temporary marker; no OBS, Decky, Flatpak, streaming or network used. Exact owned fixture process group was killed during cleanup.

facts: stop sends SIGTERM and kill_if_still_running sends SIGKILL after five seconds
sandboxed_plugin.shutdown awaits _unload before _uninstall, then stops its event loop; hook return values do not veto removal

findings.proposed_fix: Within #82, define one teardown policy for the supported loader budget; latch closing/cancellation and signal owned pending actions before the first await, bound/detach slow observation appropriately, and make abrupt backend termination safe for owned command processes. Drain/cancel all adapter-owned tasks, including configuration readers and update-check bookkeeping, without indiscriminately killing OBS or assuming hooks can veto Decky actions. Keep any surviving dependency worker's existing inherited leases and bounded recovery contract.
acceptance: A faithful five-second loader stop fixture with slow microphone/dependency observations cannot permit a pending Start to mutate after backend death/reload acknowledgement
Late spawn ownership, active stream/record/replay, unknown output and abrupt parent death are tested separately; no forced kill of ordinary OBS or unrelated processes
All tracked RPC/read/update tasks have defined shutdown behavior and no child/lease is silently orphaned
Document that hooks are best effort and cannot veto normal Decky replacement/removal; leave actual supported Decky/SteamOS execution unrun until owner test
findings.dedupe: Extend existing #82 lifecycle acceptance; do not create another broad lifecycle/refactor issue. Missing configuration-task drain is a subcase of this finding.

findings.title: Wipe deletes control/install lock inodes while holding their leases
findings.trigger: An explicitly selected legacy --wipe runs while another controller or installer starts after the wipe removes the selected state/base directory but before the operation exits its lock contexts.
findings.impact: Wipe marks the state as tree and recursively removes the currently held control.lock. A concurrent controller can create a new state/control.lock inode and acquire it while the wipe still owns the old inode. The base/install.lock is deleted similarly. This defeats serialization around the remaining deletions, and waiters with old open descriptors can form a second lock generation. Reset already preserves the control.lock inode, demonstrating a bounded model to reuse.

reproduction.safety: Only synthetic disposable state files were removed; OBS state checks were fixed idle mocks and plugin removal was disabled.

findings.proposed_fix: Keep stable coordination lock inodes outside the wipe deletion set (or preserve the minimal lock namespaces as reset already does), and make the preview truthful about retained coordination metadata. Do not unlink a live coordination path as a cleanup postcondition. Cover install and control locks together.
acceptance: A controller/installer started at each deletion boundary cannot acquire a second lock generation
Pre-existing waiters and newly opened lock descriptors serialize on the same inode
Wipe still deletes only explicitly selected owned data and preserves ordinary OBS, other plugins, shared dependencies and unselected media
Recovery after partial deletion preserves lock identity and reports remaining selected paths
findings.dedupe: A concrete legacy cleanup regression under #82, not a new removal framework.

findings.title: Retained Desktop installer mutates Flatpak dependencies before idle preflight or shared locks
findings.trigger: A user runs the retained Desktop install/repair path with one OBS/GStreamer dependency missing while output is active/unknown or a native dependency job is already holding the shared control lease.
findings.impact: ensure_dependencies can remote-add/install both references before require_idle or installation_lock/control_lock is reached. It therefore bypasses the native dependency job's idle/lease gate and can overlap that job or alter dependencies before a later safety refusal. It also trusts an existing remote solely by the name flathub and does not match the native controller's explicit trust/branch checks.

reproduction.method: Run real install composition with side-effect-free dependency marker, no-op directory preparation/locks, and an idle preflight that rejects; no package installed. Source at282–295 establishes the Flatpak mutation commands executed by that earlier stage.

findings.proposed_fix: As part of retiring mandatory paired installation in #82, keep any explicit legacy recovery path gated by validated session, fresh idle state and the same shared lease before dependency mutation; make remote/ref policy equivalent to the native setup boundary or route to that already-owned operation. Avoid a second automatic install transaction. Preserve historical archives as compatibility evidence, not permission to leave current helper entry points inconsistent.
acceptance: Active/unknown output, busy native setup and busy control lease produce no remote-add/install command
A pre-existing disabled/unverified/unrelated flathub remote is rejected before mutation
Only missing compatible refs are installed and cancellation/retry preserves shared dependencies
Normal standard ZIP installation still has no dependency download in lifecycle initialization
findings.dedupe: Bound retained helper behavior under #82 instead of duplicating completed #78 native dependency-job implementation.

findings.title: Plugin update check can recommend downgrading a newer standard Decky plugin to the old paired runtime
findings.trigger: Standard Decky plugin version9 coexists with retained Desktop app4, and the verified old paired release channel offers version5. The panel's check chooses app4 for comparison.
findings.impact: The plugin reports version5 as available even though version5 is older than the loaded plugin9, then tells the user to use the Desktop updater and repair the pair. That updater compares only the Desktop version and invokes the paired installer, which replaces the normal Decky plugin as part of its apply. The normal Decky-only install can also be directed to a Desktop updater it never installed.

reproduction.method: Disposable app4 manifest/current symlink, real releases.current_versions and check_updates with only _latest replaced by a fixed verified-shape candidate5; comparison selection exactly mirrors main.py748.

observed.message: OBSGod 0.1.0-deck.5 is available. Stop output and use Update OBSGod in Desktop Mode to install it.

reproduction.safety: No network, update or installation invoked.

findings.proposed_fix: Complete existing #82 channel alignment: treat the loaded standard plugin as the primary update identity and give truthful Decky/sideload instructions for its actual channel. Surface a separate optional legacy app status instead of declaring the pair damaged. If retained recovery can replace a newer plugin, require a deliberate version-specific recovery/downgrade action rather than presenting it as an ordinary update.
acceptance: Decky-only, matching old pair, newer-plugin/older-app, newer-app/older-plugin, offline and no-published-plugin-release cases return accurate independent statuses
No ordinary check recommends a candidate older than the loaded plugin or a missing updater
Check-only behavior remains read-only and source/repository trust does not expand
Legacy cleanup preview can retire obsolete app/launchers while preserving the active Decky plugin and shared settings by default

findings.title: Legacy path validators lack the writable-ancestor protection used by native storage
findings.trigger: Legacy installer/updater/removal roots have a user-owned group/other-writable nonsticky ancestor, such as a shared custom data directory inside the user's home.
findings.impact: Legacy validation accepts the ancestor even though another user may be able to replace descendants between validation and operations. New native storage and control paths explicitly refuse this condition. The validation gap is confirmed; no multi-user exploit or credential exposure was attempted or claimed.

reproduction.method: Create a disposable home/shared ancestor with mode0777, call paths.validate_owned_root(home/shared/obsgod,home)
reproduction.observed: Accepted without error; no installer/remover invoked.

findings.proposed_fix: If the legacy helpers remain reachable, apply the same owned/non-writable-or-sticky ancestor policy to their current writable/removal roots; share only a small validation seam where that directly eliminates demonstrated drift. Preserve supported home aliases, safe custom XDG roots and trusted sticky temporary roots.
acceptance: 0770/0777 nonsticky unsafe ancestry fails before writes/deletes/lock creation
Safe owner-only roots, supported normalized home aliases and trusted sticky ancestors work
Ancestry changes between preview and apply fail closed and unrelated sentinels are preserved
findings.dedupe: Coordinate with security auditor; merge into any matching ancestry/lock finding rather than creating duplicate cleanup work.

architecture.mode: read-only source audit; no product changes, builds, full matrix, commits or external writes
architecture.summary: The documented ownership boundaries are substantially intact. Keep the Go control/OBS layer, Python process adapters and existing React/Decky UI. The useful cleanup is a small action/deadline policy, stricter readback contracts and removal of demonstrably duplicated observations; no framework or adapter rewrite is justified.

findings.title: Align capture-mode deadline and late-completion behavior across UI, adapter and CLI
findings.evidence: The UI abandons its capture-mode promise after 15 seconds; the Promise wrapper does not cancel its RPC. Python allows 85 seconds and shields the control task; Go permits 75 seconds including the shared control-lock wait. A different CLI process holding control.lock for 15–75 seconds can therefore cause an unconfirmed UI reply before the original request acquires the lock and saves capture mode later. Backend busy/state checks still prevent this from authorizing a broadcast or competing mutation.
findings.status: Source-proven deadline mismatch and late-write path; timed real-process reproduction not run during this audit.
findings.change: Give this quick settings mutation a short backend lock/deadline policy whose complete command, cleanup and readback budget fits beneath the UI deadline, or preserve pending operation identity in the UI until authoritative completion. Extract only the small action timeout/cancellation policy used by _run and the frontend wrappers; retain special Start/Stop and microphone-lease semantics.
findings.benefit: The player can tell whether a capture-mode edit is still pending, failed without writing, or completed. A future action cannot silently acquire the wrong default timeout from unrelated stream-start behavior.
findings.risk: A generic cancellation abstraction could accidentally cancel Stop or microphone release. Keep action-specific policies and avoid replacing the existing task/state machine.
acceptance: Hold the actual shared control lock past the UI budget, invoke packaged capture-mode change, release the lock, and prove either no later settings write occurs or the same pending operation remains visible through completion.
Cover success near the deadline, caller disconnect, watcher-lease contention, Stop during the wait, and repeated identical edits; preserve key/settings binding and explicit broadcast authorization.
Ensure action timeout ordering includes Go's post-action status and Python's additional status query; testing only the core mutation timeout is insufficient.
findings.test_gap: Existing Python/browser tests cover capture-mode coalescing, JSON arguments and live/unknown output guards; they do not exercise shared-lock delay beyond the 15-second UI deadline.

findings.title: Reject incomplete successful configuration readback instead of inventing readiness
findings.evidence: A read-only Python probe passed schema_version=1, all success/readiness booleans true, settings={} and connection={} to _public_configuration. It returned ok/configured/output_known/can_configure/can_close all true with synthesized default settings and an unknown connection. Current Go does not emit that payload; this is a malformed/future-contract robustness gap, not a reproduced production write or broadcast. Separately, shipped outputKnown accepts payloads lacking output_known via a fallback whose comment names older preview fixtures.
findings.change: Require the mandatory schema-v1 settings/connection fields and mutually consistent readiness flags before granting client readiness. Retain documented optional legacy fields such as zero/omitted dimensions. Use a small shared corpus of real Go-produced and malformed JSON fixtures across Go, Python and JS; do not require schema generation or a new validation library. Review and remove the fixture-only output-known fallback once supported runtime contracts are enumerated.
findings.benefit: A missing field cannot look like a saved default or fresh safe configuration; actual contract drift becomes visible at the boundary.
findings.risk: Overstrict readback validation can reject legitimate old zero-dimension/capture-mode representations. Preserve those explicitly and keep Go as the sole write authority.
acceptance: Missing required settings/connection members, wrong member types and contradictory can_configure/can_close flags must return unknown readiness with both actions disabled.
Actual first-run, configured, running-idle, streaming, legacy-zero-dimension and unavailable Go responses retain their intended UI states.
Unknown or absent output-known data cannot enable new output or destructive/configuration controls; Stop/recovery remains available.
findings.verification: Executed only an import and pure projection call with PYTHONDONTWRITEBYTECODE=1; no child command, application data or source file was changed.

findings.disposition: measure-and-bounded-refactor-in-84; not a proven target-performance defect
findings.title: Remove repeated observations before adding another polling/cache layer
findings.evidence: One successful Status invokes RuntimeStatus twice: directly, then through ObserveMedia/mediaSnapshotFrom. RuntimeStatus performs five serial WebSocket requests. The base status path therefore performs 13 requests before optional screenshot/audio work, including GetRecordStatus three times, under a two-second budget. Source-defined frontend cadences add about 40 main status and 12 full configuration/Status CLI invocations per minute while mounted. The installed-compatible dependency readiness path executes six Flatpak queries every five seconds (up to 72 Flatpak processes/minute), even with details hidden. Opening health adds another independent five-second sample. These are call-count estimates from code, not measured Deck CPU/latency results.
findings.change: First pass the just-verified runtime ownership observation into an internal media snapshot helper, keeping independent public MediaStatus validation intact. Then measure actual packaged calls with panel open/closed and health shown/hidden. Only if useful, add a short completed-read cache/coalescing policy for installed dependency readiness with explicit invalidation after install/cancel/context change and manual refresh; keep Go's fresh Start/setup preflight authority.
findings.benefit: Removing the redundant RuntimeStatus alone takes the base status request count from 13 to 8 and reduces deadline pressure without reusing stale state. Bounded readiness polling reduces subprocess churn on the target.
findings.risk: Sharing state across separate invocations or caching edit/output authority would weaken unknown-state handling. Reuse only within one authenticated observation, and keep per-mutation fresh checks.
acceptance: Count fixture WebSocket requests and verify one runtime ownership read per Status; force each request failure and retain unknown output rather than guessed idle.
Use delayed fixture responses near the two-second budget and confirm optional media/audio work cannot convert observation failure into safe idle.
Record command counts/latency for mounted, hidden, reopened and health-expanded panel states before and after any polling change; do not claim FPS/power gains without Deck measurement.

Dependency install/cancel/reload/context changes and explicit refresh invalidate cached readiness; external dependency removal is discovered within a documented bound and fresh Start still rejects it.
findings.test_gap: Current runtime fixture responds immediately; it checks independent recording/capture facts without an observation call-count or slow-response assertion.

findings.disposition: small-later-cleanup; do not delay owner testing
findings.title: Move the two reusable package helpers out of the legacy executable builder
findings.evidence: The primary standard Decky builder imports the entire executable legacy package-deck.py module through importlib only to call capture_source and notices. Shared payload/ZIP/staging logic already lives in decky_package.py. The dependency makes an unrelated compatibility-builder top-level edit able to break the primary builder. No current artifact corruption or unsafe import side effect was found.
findings.change: Move just capture_source and notices into an appropriate existing/shared packaging module, retain thin call compatibility for the older builder, and remove dynamic primary-to-legacy import. Remove unused stream_health Result/embedded branches only after confirming all supported producers; they are not a separate cleanup project.
findings.benefit: Primary packaging has a direct dependency on neutral helpers, while the compatibility archive remains supported.
findings.risk: Changing notices/order/archive timestamps changes package hashes; expected byte-preserving extraction needs equivalence checks at the same epoch and pinned dependencies.
acceptance: Before/after helper outputs and all standard payload files match byte-for-byte at fixed source inputs/epoch; notices/preferred-source contents remain complete.
Retain primary official-CLI assembly coverage and legacy runtime/updater compatibility tests; do not remove the legacy builder or old public artifacts merely because the standard ZIP is primary.

ownership_and_refactor_notes: steamdeck/decky/main.py is 799 lines and owns subprocess lifecycle, action serialization, public configuration projection, setup integration and update checks. Split pure projection/validation and the bounded action/process policy only when addressing ARCH-01/02; preserve Plugin as the orchestration owner. Its length alone does not justify a rewrite.

internal/deck/control.go is 781 lines. Start/TestRecording/media.go repeat capture preparation and watcher setup, but different rollback/preexisting-output semantics are intentional. An extraction must encode those ownership differences explicitly; defer broad workflow unification until a demonstrated regression/change need.

findings.title: Put observed status and Start/Stop at the top of the normal panel
findings.status: Observed source order and reproduced with packaged frontend; target usability inference
findings.observation: Dependency setup, the complete saved destination form and local connection section all render before YOUR STREAM even for an already configured/live user. In the 400x800 native-stub fixture, configured-idle Start y=1812px / Stop y=1865px and document height=5763px. After configuration also refreshed to live state, Start y=1786px / Stop y=1839px, so the primary stream controls remain off the initial viewport. First-run Start y=1942px. Advanced mixer controls and between-game/media controls are mostly expanded below.
findings.impact: Routine streaming and urgent Stop/recover require unnecessary navigation past setup/recovery content. The normal QAM feels like an administrative form rather than stream control.
findings.suggested_fix: Reuse native Decky components; move the compact observed stream status and Start/Stop before setup. Show a concise setup-required next step for first use; collapse saved destination, dependency details and local connection/advanced controls behind explicit disclosures. Keep live mute near primary controls. Keep Stop/recover reachable independent of setup readiness and do not make the decorative mark carry state.
acceptance: Configured idle/live/unknown panels expose status plus relevant Start/Stop/recover in their initial target QAM view.
Controller navigation reaches Stop without traversing setup fields; no focus jump on polls or disclosure collapse.
Unknown/stale/output-active and setup-busy safety remains unchanged; first-use setup remains discoverable and does not broadcast.
Use a focused browser geometry/navigation check plus actual Deck controller/Steam keyboard acceptance; native-stub geometry is not the target proof.

findings.title: A recovery transport failure has no visible result while stream-health details are closed
findings.status: Reproduced fault injection in actual packaged frontend
findings.observation: Retry bounded audio/capture recovery catches rejection into HealthTools.message, but that message only renders inside the open health-details block. With the default closed state, an injected retry_recovery rejection makes one backend call and produces no failure text or failure toast. The root tool runner clears busy but does not retain a failure notice on rejection.
findings.impact: The user gets no explanation or next action after a failed recovery attempt and can repeat it without knowing the outcome is unconfirmed.
findings.suggested_fix: Render the recovery action result next to its button regardless of health disclosure state and expose a visible status/live result for pending, success and unconfirmed failure. Preserve the actual observed output state and bounded backend behavior.
acceptance: Reject the recovery callable with health details closed and open; a visible, accessible, secret-free failure explains that recovery is unconfirmed and offers inspect/retry guidance.
No green success, stopped state or restart is inferred from the request result.

findings.title: Saved-clip browser reports an empty library before listing has finished
findings.status: Reproduced delayed response in actual packaged frontend
findings.observation: Browse saved clips opens immediately with clips initialized to an empty array. During an unresolved media list call it renders 'No finalized managed clips listed' and Desktop inspection advice. There is no distinct list-loading state; a later result can replace this apparent empty state.
findings.impact: Users can believe clips are missing and leave or repeat work while the first observation is still pending. Existing cached results similarly have no explicit freshness indicator during reload.
findings.suggested_fix: Track clip-list loading, loaded-empty and failure separately; show the empty message only after a successful completed empty list. Preserve previous clips with a refreshing indicator rather than claiming current completeness.
acceptance: A delayed list shows 'Loading saved clips…' or equivalent until completion.
Completed nonempty, completed empty, rejected and subsequent refresh states have distinct appropriate text without losing prior confirmed clips or starting output.

findings.title: Provider guide navigation lacks error feedback
findings.status: Reproduced with repository external-navigation failure flag
findings.observation: The destination guide button directly calls NavigateToExternalWeb. With fixture.linkFailure=true it raises 'fixture external navigation denied' as a page error and renders no failure message. The Support component already uses a bounded catch-and-message pattern for the same navigation API.
findings.impact: First-time users who cannot open the guide get no in-panel reason or recovery instruction while collecting server/key details.
findings.suggested_fix: Use a small shared or local guarded navigation handler with provider-specific, secret-free feedback and retry/manual URL guidance. Keep local setup usable offline.
acceptance: Rejected external navigation preserves focus, shows an accessible provider-guide failure, and leaves server/key drafts and broadcast state intact.
Successful navigation opens only after explicit user action.

findings.title: Advanced options point to optional Desktop Setup without a route from the plugin
findings.status: Observed source integration gap; actual target journey unrun
findings.observation: Configuration supports an optional onOpenDesktopSetup button, but Content never supplies the callback. Multiple native hints direct users to Desktop Setup for idle media, profile import/bindings and recording storage, while only the documentation explains running the bundled bin/obsgod deck setup. The standard ZIP carries setup assets but no separately installed Desktop launcher.
findings.impact: Users reaching the bounds of native controls have an avoidable dead end and may install a second app or assume the advanced feature is missing.
findings.suggested_fix: Provide a bounded 'Open Desktop Setup / how to open' help route consistent with actual Desktop/Gaming Mode lifecycle. A clear instruction page using the existing bundled command is sufficient before any more elaborate launcher; private loopback tokens must stay private. Update stale quality guidance now that exact native quality fields exist.
acceptance: From the installed standard plugin a user can discover exact optional Desktop Setup instructions without a separately installed application or development tools.
The route uses the existing protected local setup; no token enters diagnostics, no implicit provider login and no output begins.

findings.title: Standalone-plugin update guidance still promises a bundled Desktop updater
findings.status: Observed source and package inventory mismatch; actual Decky update acceptance unrun
findings.observation: The update failure message and persistent UPDATES hint tell users to use the bundled Desktop updater. The inspected 33-file primary standard ZIP includes the runtime and optional browser setup but contains no update.py or updater launcher. The compatibility Desktop runtime archive contains those files separately; canonical package docs already call Decky-managed replacement/removal primary.
